questions.q: Why is 'fully understand how SQL Pete generates SQL' a poor research question for this case study?
options: It's too easy to answer in four lessons
SQL Pete is a closed-weight model, so it can't be inspected at all
It has no stopping condition — there's no single experiment that would let you say the question is answered
Interpretability can only be done on reward models, not generative models
questions.explain: A scoped question needs a concrete pass/fail answer within the available time. 'Understand the model' is an open-ended goal, not a researchable question with a stopping condition.

questions.q: What two models are the candidate targets for this chapter's interpretability case study?
options: SQL Pete from Chapter 4 and the Project 2 reward model from Chapter 3
Two different checkpoints of Project 1's RL policy
The SFT-only checkpoint compared against itself
A 7B model and a 1.5B model, both newly trained for this chapter
questions.explain: Both SQL Pete and the Project 2 reward model are open-weight and already built, making them the two realistic candidates sitting on disk by Chapter 5.

questions.q: Why does SQL Pete fit the activation-patching method (Lesson 22) better than the Project 2 reward model does?
options: SQL Pete is a smaller model, so patching is computationally cheaper
Activation patching only works on encoder-only architectures
The reward model's single scalar output on one forward pass gives no second output token to compare against, unlike a generation that can be compared token by token
The Project 2 reward model has no open weights at all
questions.explain: Activation patching needs two runs that differ in one output, so a component's activation can be swapped and the effect measured. A classifier's single scalar score doesn't offer that same token-by-token comparison as cleanly as a generation does.

questions.q: What specific, already-measured behavior does this chapter commit to investigating in SQL Pete?
options: The exact learning rate used during RLHF
Whether SQL Pete can answer questions outside Northwind and AdventureWorks2012
The surface-polish bias from Lesson 13
Schema hallucination — referencing a column or table name that doesn't exist in the schema — from Lesson 19
questions.explain: Lesson 19 already measured a schema-hallucination rate on held-out failures, giving this chapter a concrete, falsifiable behavior to chase rather than an open-ended search.

questions.q: Why does starting from a known, measured behavior difference beat starting from an unguided search through a model's internals?
options: Known behaviors are always caused by a single attention head
A known behavior gives you a hypothesis with a built-in falsifier: if patching the suspected component doesn't change the behavior, the hypothesis is cleanly wrong
It doesn't matter — any starting point works equally well
Unguided searches are faster to run
questions.explain: Starting from a measured regression lets you form a specific causal hypothesis and test it directly, rather than hoping something interesting turns up in an open-ended search with no clear way to know if you looked hard enough.
